paper.citation: O'Bryan KR, Doering TM, Morton RW, Coffey VG, Phillips SM, Cox GR. Do multi-ingredient protein supplements augment resistance training-induced gains in skeletal muscle mass and strength? A systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 trials. Br J Sports Med. 2020;54:573-581.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 35 randomised trials (1387 participants, 6 to 78 weeks of resistance training) comparing multi-ingredient protein (MIP) supplements with non-MIP or protein-only controls. MIP supplements produced greater gains in total body mass, fat-free mass and upper and lower body 1RM than non-MIP supplements, but were not superior to protein-only supplements for lean mass or strength.
paper.tldr: Across 35 trials, multi-ingredient protein supplements added modest gains in fat-free mass and strength over non-MIP controls during resistance training, but did not outperform protein alone and increased fat mass compared with protein only.
paper.methods: Systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and SPORTDiscus to October 2017 for randomised trials of at least 6 weeks of resistance training with an MIP supplement in healthy, non-energy-restricted adults. Random-effects meta-analyses were run in RevMan on change-score means and SDs, with subgroup analyses by training status and age and GRADE quality ratings; nine trials with more than three high or unclear risk-of-bias domains were excluded from the meta-analyses.
paper.findings: Compared with all non-MIP supplements, MIP increased total body mass (MD 1.23 kg, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.70), fat-free mass (MD 0.80 kg, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.15), 1RM upper body (MD 2.56 kg, 95% CI 0.79 to 4.33) and 1RM lower body (MD 4.22 kg, 95% CI 0.79 to 7.64), with no difference in fat mass. Compared with protein-only supplements, MIP increased fat mass (MD 0.76 kg, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.40) with no difference in total body mass, fat-free mass or 1RM.
paper.limitations: Only English-language RCTs were included, with moderate statistical heterogeneity, small trials (6 to 69 participants), protein doses from 10 to 101 g per day, and varied supplement composition. Several trials were at unclear or high risk of bias, training status was unreported in some, and the authors disclosed that a dairy-industry agency supported some included trials. Most outcomes were rated moderate quality.
paper.practicalImplications: If an MIP product is used, it should contain a substantial amount of protein. MIP products offer modest additional gains over non-MIP controls, but protein-only products performed similarly for lean mass and strength, so total protein intake remains the core strategy.
paper.athleteDev: For strength and power training, MIP products may add small gains in lean mass and strength over non-protein controls, but they do not beat protein alone. Staff should prioritise total protein intake and the training programme, and monitor the extra fat mass seen with MIP compared with protein only.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, and its participants were healthy adults, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.
